definitions.definition: Cyber security is the practice of defending computers, servers, mobile devices, electronic systems, networks and data from malicious attacks.
Confidentiality is preventing the disclosure of data to unauthorized parties, keeping shared data private and anonymous.
Integrity is protecting information from being modified by unauthorized parties.
Availability is making sure that authorized parties are able to access the information when needed.
A vulnerability is a weakness or lacuna in a policy, procedure, protocol, hardware or software that has the potential to cause damage or loss.
A threat is a possible security violation that might exploit the vulnerability of a system or asset.
Risk is the product of threat probability and the potential loss that may result.
An active attack is a network exploit in which a hacker attempts to make changes to data on the target or data en route to the target.
A passive attack makes use of information from the system without affecting system resources, e.g. eavesdropping and traffic analysis.
Malware (malicious code) is software designed to take over or damage a computer user's operating system without the user's knowledge or approval.
A virus is a program that attempts to damage a computer system and replicate itself to other computer systems, requiring a host file to replicate.
A worm is a self-replicating program that infects one system and spreads to other systems on the network, e.g. Code Red.
A Trojan horse is a malicious program disguised as legitimate software that cannot replicate itself and often carries spying or backdoor functions.
A logic bomb is malware that lies dormant until a trigger activity, such as a specific date or program launch, activates it; it does not self-replicate.
A denial of service (DoS) attack deprives users of access to a network or web resource by overwhelming the target with more traffic than it can handle.
Spoofing is a situation in which one person or program successfully masquerades as another by falsifying information to gain an illegitimate advantage.
IP spoofing is the creation of IP packets with a forged source address to conceal the sender's identity or impersonate another computing system.
A security policy is the set of rules and practices that regulate how an organization manages and protects its computing and communication resources.
Non-repudiation offers a guarantee against denial by a party that it created or sent a particular message.
Cyberspace is the electronic medium of digital networks used to store, modify and communicate information, including the Internet.
Cyber warfare is the use of digital attacks, like computer viruses and hacking, by a nation-state to disrupt the vital computer systems of another.
Cyber terrorism is the convergence of cyberspace and terrorism—unlawful attacks against computers and networks to intimidate or coerce a government or its people.
Cyber espionage is the act of obtaining secrets without the permission and knowledge of the holder, via the Internet, for personal, economic, political or military advantage.
Computer forensics involves the preservation, identification, extraction, documentation and interpretation of computer media for evidentiary and root cause analysis.
Digital evidence is any information, subject to human intervention or not, that can be extracted from a computer.
SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is a set of communication guidelines that allow software to transmit electronic mail over the Internet.
S/MIME is a security-enhanced version of MIME that provides digital signatures and encryption of Internet messages.
Admissibility of evidence refers to the legal rules that determine whether potential evidence can be considered by a court.
A mobile device is easy to use, enables remote access to business networks and the Internet, and enables quick transfer of data.
In a push attack, the attacker creates malicious code at the user's mobile device by hacking it and then spreads it to other elements of the network.
The Cabir worm is malware that infects mobile phones running Symbian OS and spreads to other phones using wireless Bluetooth signals.
A security breach is the unauthorized acquisition of data that compromises the security, confidentiality and integrity of personal information.
An insider threat is the misuse or destruction of sensitive or confidential information and IT equipment by employees, contractors and other trusted individuals.
Copyright is a right given by law to creators of literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works, and to producers of films and sound recordings, to do or authorize certain acts with their creations.
A trademark is a distinctive sign used by a business to uniquely identify itself and its products or services, and to distinguish them from other businesses.
A patent is a legal monopoly granted to the owner of a new invention for a limited period of time; it can be granted for a product as well as a process.
Digital rights management (DRM) is a systematic approach to copyright protection for digital media that prevents unauthorized redistribution and restricts copying.
Spamdexing (search engine spamming) is the practice of creating websites that will be illegitimately indexed with a high position in search engines.
Data privacy is the part of the data protection area that deals with the proper handling of data based on its relative importance.
Personally identifiable information (PII) can be used to distinguish or trace an individual's identity, alone or when combined with other linking information.
The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a legal framework setting guidelines for the collection and processing of personal information of individuals in the European Union.
A privacy notice (privacy statement) is a statement made to a data subject describing how the organization collects, uses, retains and discloses personal information.
Data masking ensures data is stored or transmitted with only the minimal details required for a specific transaction, with other details masked or omitted.
Data linking brings together information from different sources to create a new, richer dataset by identifying and combining corresponding records.
In the restrictive sense, cybercrime (computer crime) is any illegal behavior carried out by means of electronic methods targeting the security of computer systems and data processed by them.
In the general sense, a computer-related crime is any illegal behavior committed by means of, or in relation to, a computer system or network.
Under Section 2 of the IT Act, a computer is any electronic, magnetic, optical or other high-speed data processing device performing logical, arithmetic and memory functions.
Under the IT Act, a computer resource means a computer, computer system, computer network, data, computer database or software.
Under the IT Act, an intermediary is any person who on behalf of another person receives, stores or transmits an electronic message or provides a service with respect to it.
The IT Act 2000 provides legal recognition for transactions carried out by means of electronic data interchange and other electronic communication (electronic commerce).
